<Rep. Robert Garcia>: Democrats strongly oppose H.R. 5172, the so-called Strong Sentences for Safer D.C. Streets Act. This bill would impose new, aggressive mandatory minimum sentencing in the District of Columbia.
Yet again, this bill ignores the will of D.C. residents and the existing research on mandatory minimum sentencing. We know that decades of evidence shows that mandatory minimum sentencing laws have failed to reduce crime, and in many ways, worsened problems within our justice system.
One of the clearest outcomes of mandatory minimum sentencing laws has been the exponential increase in the United States prison population. The result of tough-on-crime legislation from the 90s was mass incarceration, not meaningful or lasting reductions in crime. Research shows no evidence that mandatory minimums significantly reduce crime rates.
Research instead points to the conclusion that it is the certainty of punishment, not the severity, that deters crime. We need more police, more detectives, and more effective prosecutions, not longer sentences alone.
Over the last two decades, both the federal government and the states have begun to move away from mandatory minimum sentencing. This has been a bipartisan push. Republicans who championed this issue included Ted Cruz, Mike Lee, John Cornyn, and many others.
Beyond its limited crime control impact, increasing mandatory minimum sentencing makes our legal system less effective. Judges lose discretion to consider mitigating circumstances or propose alternative punishments. Mandatory minimum sentencing also disproportionately affects minority groups. It is a racial justice issue. At the federal level, mandatory minimum sentencing is rarely applied to most violent crimes.
We must learn from our past. Mandatory minimum sentencing has fueled mass incarceration, failed to deter crime, and deepened racial disparities.
Robert Garcia,
Ranking Member.
